chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Falling pop sales, disco and the end of the fad
summary: Wilson notes pop sales are down while jazz and classical hold steady, mocks disco strings, and predicts the pop era will run its course.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: One thing that's puzzling, I was just reading in that magazine, Billboard over there, the sales of that pop thing are down, these little record companies are firing about 1,000 people, but the jazz and classical are holding their own. They never were that big, but they don't have a big dip in jazz and classical sales -- but the pop companies are really having headaches with sales. Now, the guys who were selling gold records a year or two ago can't give their stuff away right now. They were working with the fad at the moment, and they haven't found a new fad to capitalize on.

Just like with the disco -- the disco music with that heavy beat, you know, getting the string sections from the New York Philharmonic, putting a rock rhythm section behind it -- you know, no musician in their right mind would ever do that! A businessman would, though; he say5/ well, that will sell, so do it. Tiger Joe somebody on the drums here and get some people from the Philharmonic on the violins -- because that might sell, see. But a musician wouldn't do that. That's the type of music they been producing for 20 years now.
Yeah. Well, do you hold out any hope that perhaps with -- you might get some young people right out of college ...

Well, it has to run its course. See, these people are milking the situation dry; the validity of this whole pop movement we're in now, the point had been made in 1958, see, when the Beatles were popular, they were the last of that phase -- but I guess Presley would be the peak of it, I'd say, Johnny Ray and Presley and the Four This and the Four That -- you know, the groups in the early fifties.
But then since 1958 or so, the businessmen have just been milking every nickel that they can get out of the whole disco idea and everything like that.

And of course, they manipulate the public taste by controlling the records that are played on the radio, and creating the whole wave that everybody has to go along with, you get on the bandwagon and everybody wants to make some money, they have to go with this whole big program.

But it will just run its course naturally, and I think it's beginning to fall apart now. The only thing that can come now, if they can't think of any more gimmicks or tricks, is music. Because more and more now, you see the 'easy listening stations' are coming in vogue, they're sneaking more and more of those on the air now, coming in with those big bands with a lot of violins, and at least,

it's musicians playing and not a bunch of something or other -- these are guys blowing a horn or playing a violin or something, and it's more the big, now the new wave, I understand, they're beginning to play a lot of the old big band music on the radio. More and more stations are beginning to program Glenn Miller and Artie Shaw and some of the old stuff.
